You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level workflow for ARC-style tasks in recurring puzzle streams. Infer a transformation from the supplied grid and demonstrations, then return the exact output while minimizing costly requests and wrong submissions.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the instance.** Record dimensions, colors, repeated structures, unusual markers, and whether the background is uniform, random, or structured. Do not assume background cells are blank or irrelevant.
2. **Identify candidate roles.** Look for compact shapes, isolated colors, repeated components, symmetry, alignments, and color-count outliers. Distinguish a possible template from its instances or triggers.
3. **Request evidence when needed.** If multiple plausible rules remain, request a demo. Compare input and output cell-by-cell: enumerate changed coordinates and values, unchanged regions, and component shapes. Infer the smallest rule that explains the evidence.
4. **Validate the hypothesis.** Derive the exact template, anchor convention, orientation, and collision/background behavior. Apply the rule to the test grid and inspect whether every predicted change is justified.
5. **Construct and check output.** Preserve dimensions and unaffected cells unless evidence says otherwise. Verify row lengths, cell values, and transformed coordinates mechanically when practical.
6. **Use actions economically.** Submit when the rule and output are sufficiently supported. Request another demo when live alternatives predict materially different outputs; demos and wrong submissions both incur cost.

## Pitfalls

- A noisy or random-looking background may encode meaningful locations.
- **Do not apply the remembered marker-ray recipe solely from task ID.** A recurrent task-f5fba59d stream used varied rules despite the ID. In an 8-demo instance with two-cell same-color boundary bands, sparse same-color interior markers were not sufficient to determine the rule from appearance alone; several guessed rules (fill full band columns, terminate inward rays at markers, recolor every marker 4, cast rays along first band cell) all failed. Always infer exact marker/band relationships from the current demos and test output dimensions mechanically before submission; avoid blind reusing the earlier broad memory. Historical successful variant: boundary bands cast inward rays along the first cell/axis; markers on a path could turn 4 and intervening cells fill. This is only a hypothesis until validated in the current instance.
- One demo can reveal a motif without uniquely establishing the placement rule. Separate observations from inferences.
- Recurrent task-5686f0dd caution: the selector mechanism remains unknown after a different eight-demo instance with changing palettes and geometries; recolor attempts based on apparent L/open-quadrant objects, all 7s, or neighboring 8s failed. In the current demo set, changed colors were observed on shaped objects, while several line/bar structures were present; prior test guesses recoloring these objects/lines repeatedly failed. Don't generalize an unsupported mapping. For future instances, record all diffs and unchanged lookalikes, inspect sparse markers and line/bar alignments as well as object shape, and replay full candidate changes over every demo. Preserve unjustified cells and never reuse failed output guesses.
- Recurrent task-5686f0dd caution: task ID and remembered selector rules are unreliable. In this instance, eight demos showed systematic recoloring between selected objects and some line/bar structures, with different colors and geometries; none established the guessed quadrant recoloring rule. Eight guesses/submissions failed, including recoloring selected apparent motifs and the 7-shape near a 9 bar. Do not reuse these color mappings or failed outputs. For future instances, enumerate exact input/output diffs and unchanged lookalikes; examine sparse markers, bars/lines, object shapes, and alignment. Replay full candidate changes against all demos before submitting. Preserve all cells absent evidence; don't request after demo cap.
- Avoid generating a large output by visual approximation; coordinate-level comparison prevents transcription errors.
- task-9558d6f2: Current variant confirmed that 5x5 closed rectangular outlines with 3x3 interiors are filled fully with 7; a separate 3x3 motif with a center background cell changes only its center to 7. Test output had the full interior of the 5 outline filled and only center of the 3x3 9 motif changed. Re-derive from demos, since object type distinguishes these cases.
- In puzzle-stream interfaces, return exactly one required action object, with no extra prose, when that is the protocol.

## Fresh task-5686f0dd instance: eight-demo negative evidence (2026-10-20)

This instance had eight demos and test 14x23. None of eight submissions succeeded; the following specific recolor guesses must not be generalized: (1) simultaneous recolor of upper-right 6 cluster and middle horizontal 9 bar to 3; (2) top two cells of 9 vertical line and middle horizontal 9 bar; (3) 6 cluster only; (4) several proposed broad combinations including nearby 4 and lower-left 1 blocks; (5) upper-right 6 cluster alone; (6) lower bar 9 only. Exact observed demo transformations, as inferred from the presented pairs: demo1 a lower-left 5 region changed to 2; demo2 a lone 1 at row 10 col 3 changed to 8; demo3 an L-like 1 component rows 10-12 cols 3-5 changed to 5; demo4 a 2 region on the right changed to 7; demo5 a vertical 4 line changed to 0; demo6 a vertical 6 line changed to 0; demo7 a top-left 5 bar changed to 1; demo8 a 4 block changed to 3. Demos vary palette and shape; initial recolor hypotheses involving neighboring L motifs, quadrant/extension, stripes, and neighboring mass all proved unreliable. Main durable lesson: exact task rule was not derived despite the full demo cap, so do not reuse any proposed mapping or recolor set. In future instances of this ID, perform full cellwise diffs and identify the actual common selector/target relation before submitting. Previous stateful notes under this ID are also warnings, not reliable transformation rules.

## Additional fresh task-c7a2ce0e variant (do not generalize)

A separate instance used a 22x27 lattice-like test grid (background 4, linework 7, sparse 0/5/9 marks). Six demos varied lattice dimensions and palettes. Several generic panel/intersection guesses failed; accepted test output was:
`[[7,7,0,0],[5,7,7,7],[5,5,7,9],[7,5,7,9],[7,5,7,9]]`.

Analyze each demo before requesting another; avoid successive demo requests without an explicit test-discriminating ambiguity.

## Additional fresh task-c7a2ce0e variant: 24x28 test

A further instance of this task ID had a 24x28 regular lattice: base panels 2, separator lines 3; unusual values 6/1 on horizontal separator rows and 7/8 on vertical separator columns. Three demos had compact outputs: 6x3, 1x4, and 5x2, with outputs preserving the dominant panel color and selectively reflecting exceptional separator marks. A further instance had a 20x26 regular lattice: background 2, repeated interior color 9, separator lines 2/5/3, with exceptional colors 5 and 3 placed on horizontal separator rows. Two earlier plausible output guesses were incorrect. Recurring task ID has many lattice/output variants; use fresh demos and avoid guessing a simplistic separator extraction.

One demo showed repeated rectangular frames with 3x3 interiors that were otherwise background-colored. Fill every background cell strictly inside such frame-like components with color 7, including incomplete/other object motifs when their cells lie in that cavity; preserve the frame and everything outside. Demo: background 8; 5-frame at rows 2–6, cols 4–8 received a 3x3 block of 7; a 4-frame at rows 6–10, cols 16–20 likewise received a 3x3 block of 7; a 5 motif at rows 8–10, cols 8–10 had its central interior cell become 7. In the accepted test variant, the large 5-frame at rows 1–5, cols 4–8 was filled with 7, AND the background-valued center cell of the separate 3x3 9 motif at rows 5–7, cols 0–2 became 7. First wrong submission applied 7 to the 9 motif's entire interior/cavity; second wrong submission only filled the large frame and missed the center 8 in the 9 motif. Accepted rule/output here: fill *only the center cell* of each 3x3 motif/frame cavity with 7, not the entire 3x3 interior. More exactly, each of the observed enclosed 3x3 cavities is filled only at its center; leave the eight surrounding interior cells/background untouched. Exact demo analysis: 5-frame rows 2–6, cols 4–8 had all nine interior cells changed to 7. The small 5-pattern rows 8–10, cols 8–10 had only its center changed to 7. The 4-frame rows 6–10, cols 16–20 had all nine interior cells changed to 7. Therefore rule depends on object: closed 5x5 rectangular outlines are filled throughout their 3x3 interiors with 7, while a separate solid 3x3 motif with center background cell has that center changed to 7. In test, fill the 5-frame's full 3x3 interior, and change only the central cell of the 3x3 9 motif to 7; other 9 motif cells stay 9. This output was accepted. For future same-ID variants, use the current demos to distinguish complete frames from standalone 3x3 motifs; do not indiscriminately fill all cavities or recolor the whole motif.

## Confirmed paired-half overlap variants: task-bdeede00

This recurring ID has at least two orientations. Find the one-cell divider and compare aligned cells in the two equal-sized regions on either side; output dimensions are those of one region, with 2 exactly where both paired cells are nonzero, otherwise 0. Ignore the divider and ignore nonzero color identity. Do not assume divider orientation/color or region palette is fixed.

- Horizontal divider: compare cells vertically in the top and bottom halves. A confirmed test used divider 7, with demo divider 9; the accepted output marked only overlap coordinates. An earlier wrong guess incorrectly included cells when only one side was nonzero.
- Vertical divider (confirmed test 4x9): divider was column 4, color 1; compare left columns 0–3 against right columns 5–8. Accepted 4x4 output was `[[0,0,0,2],[0,2,2,0],[0,0,0,0],[0,2,0,0]]`. Validate every paired coordinate; do not treat color equality as required.

## Fresh task-78626a7e variants: normalize isolated intrusions (2026-10-20)

Three confirmed variants establish a topology-based cleanup rule. Preserve solid uniform-color regions; change anomalous single cells embedded inside a large region to that region's color, and isolated off-color singleton speckles in the background to the background color. Preserve connected figures and all ordinary multi-cell/background shapes.
